title: Periodic Table and Periodicity
tagline: The modern table, the trends it predicts, and the exceptions that earn the extra marks.

overview.intro: The periodic table is a compact statement of atomic structure: elements are ordered by nuclear charge, and their properties repeat because their electron arrangements repeat. This chapter works through the law behind that arrangement, the classification into s, p, d and f blocks, and then each property in turn — size, ionisation energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic character and oxidation state — always as a pair of directions, a reason and a named example. The exceptions of the second period are treated as part of the pattern rather than as interruptions, because that is how the examiner uses them.

facts.label: Modern periodic law
facts.value: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

facts.label: Shape of the table
facts.value: 7 periods, 18 groups, arranged as s, p, d and f blocks.

facts.label: Periodic radius
facts.value: Covalent radius of chlorine 0.99 Å; atomic radius falls across a period.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Trend, reason and example triads; anomalies of period 2 recur every year.

learningOutcomes: State the modern periodic law and explain why atomic number replaced atomic mass as the basis of classification.
Describe the construction of the long form of the periodic table and locate elements by block, group and period.
Predict the direction of change of atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity with reasons.
Explain the anomalous behaviour of the second period and compare named pairs of elements.
Relate electronic configuration to valency, oxidation state and metallic character.

learn.title: From Mendeleev to the modern periodic law

blocks.text: Mendeleev arranged the known elements in order of atomic mass and grouped those with similar properties, leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and predicting their properties with striking accuracy. Two problems remained: isotopes broke the mass order, and several pairs were out of sequence in mass yet similar in behaviour. The modern law, formulated by Moseley from X-ray experiments, states that the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. Because atomic number counts protons, it fixes the electron arrangement and therefore the chemistry, and it never splits into isotopes. The result is the long form: seven periods set by the number of occupied shells, eighteen groups defined by the outer-electron pattern, and four blocks named for the sub-shell being filled.

items: Mendeleev predicted eka-aluminium, eka-silicon and eka-boron, later found as gallium, germanium and scandium.
Atomic number removed the two defects of the mass-based law: isotopic mass inversion and the argon-potassium anomaly.
Group number for s and p blocks equals the number of valence electrons; for d blocks it counts (n−1)d plus ns electrons.
The lanthanoids and actinoids are shown below the table because inserting them would make it unwieldy.
Valency usually equals the number of unpaired valence electrons, and oxidation state is the charge an atom appears to carry.

items.text: Argon (Z = 18) has greater atomic mass than potassium (Z = 19)
items.note: Ordering by atomic number keeps potassium after argon, matching their chemistry.

items.text: Germanium filled the gap Mendeleev left for eka-silicon
items.note: Its density and oxide formula matched the prediction, which validated the grouping.

blocks.text: Radius is measured differently depending on the bonding: covalent radius is half the distance between bonded identical atoms, metallic radius half the distance between neighbours in a metal crystal, and ionic radius the radius of an ion in a lattice. Across a period the number of shells is fixed while nuclear charge rises, so the outer shell is pulled in and the atom shrinks; down a group each element adds a whole shell, and that outweighs the extra protons, so the atom grows. Ions follow the same logic plus one extra rule: a cation is smaller than its atom because a shell or an outer layer is lost, while an anion is larger because the same nucleus now holds more electrons that repel each other. Across an isoelectronic series, size falls as nuclear charge rises.

items: Across a period from sodium to chlorine, covalent radius falls steadily from 1.86 Å to 0.99 Å.
Down group 1 the atomic radius grows from 1.52 Å for lithium to 2.72 Å for caesium.
Cations are smaller and anions larger than their parent atoms.
Isoelectronic species such as N3−, O2−, F−, Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ all hold 10 electrons, so size falls as protons increase.
Noble gases are quoted as van der Waals radii, which are larger than covalent radii because no bond is formed.

items.note: The entire third shell is lost, so the ion is far smaller than the atom.
The same 17 protons now restrain 18 electrons, so the cloud expands.

items.meaning: Half the internuclear distance between two identical bonded atoms.
Effective radius of an ion in a crystal lattice, larger for anions than cations.
Species with the same number of electrons, compared by nuclear charge.
Reduction of effective nuclear pull on outer electrons by inner-shell electrons.

learn.title: Ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity

blocks.text: Three energy quantities describe how an atom holds its electrons, and all three follow the size trend because a small atom holds its electrons close to the nucleus. Ionisation energy is the energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms; successive ionisation energies rise steeply because each removal leaves a more positive ion. Electron affinity is the energy released when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one mole of electrons, and it is most exothermic for the halogens, whose near-full shell completes itself on arrival. Electronegativity is not a measurable energy at all but the ability of a bonded atom to attract the shared pair, peaking at fluorine. Each trend has a period-2 exception caused by the special stability of half-filled and filled sub-shells, and by the repulsion between electrons forced into the same small 2p orbital.

items: Ionisation energy rises across a period and falls down a group.
A sharp jump in successive ionisation energies marks the removal of a core electron: aluminium gives a big jump after the third.
Electron affinity is generally negative; noble gases and group 2 elements show positive or near-zero values because the incoming electron enters a filled or sub-filled level.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, with fluorine the highest at 4.0.
Nitrogen has a higher first ionisation energy than oxygen because its 2p^3 sub-shell is half-filled while oxygen must break a paired 2p electron.
Beryllium exceeds boron and neon exceeds fluorine in first ionisation energy for the same filled-sub-shell reason.

items.text: Removing the fourth electron from aluminium costs far more than the third
items.note: The first three are valence electrons; the fourth comes from an inner shell shielded by the others.

items.text: Chlorine releases more energy on gaining an electron than sodium does
items.note: Its small size and high effective nuclear charge stabilise the arriving electron strongly.

blocks.caption: Trend summary across period 3
rows: Electrons held more tightly in a smaller atom
Valence electrons approach a full octet

learn.title: Using periodicity: metallic character, diagonal relationships and exam reasoning

blocks.text: Periodicity becomes useful only when it is applied. Metallic character, the readiness to lose electrons, falls across a period and grows down a group, which is why caesium is the most metallic element and fluorine the least. Reactivity of metals follows the ease of electron loss, so group 1 becomes more vigorous down the group; reactivity of non-metals follows the ease of electron gain, so group 17 becomes milder down the group. A second pattern, the diagonal relationship, appears because a small, highly charged ion in period 2 resembles the heavier ion below-right of it: lithium behaves like magnesium, beryllium like aluminium, and boron like silicon, because charge density rather than group alone controls behaviour.

items: Diagonal relationship: Li ~ Mg, Be ~ Al, B ~ Si, arising from similar charge-to-size ratios.
Amphoteric oxides appear where metallic character is intermediate, as with Al2O3 and BeO.
Oxides become more acidic across a period: Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
Always state trend, reason and a named pair; three parts, three marks.

items.text: Lithium forms a nitride directly while sodium does not
items.note: Li+ is small and highly polarising, resembling Mg2+ across the diagonal.

items.text: Aluminium dissolves in both sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid
items.note: Its oxide and metal show the amphoteric behaviour typical of the Be–Al diagonal pair.

items.meaning: Tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions; increases down a group.
Similarity of period 2 elements with the element below-right of them.
Able to react with both acids and bases, as aluminium oxide does.
Readiness of an atom to lose electrons and become a cation.

keyPoints: Modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number, not atomic mass.
Seven periods equal the number of occupied shells; group number gives valence electrons in the s and p blocks.
Radius decreases across a period and increases down a group; cations shrink, anions expand.
Isoelectronic size falls as nuclear charge rises: N3− > O2− > F− > Na+ > Mg2+ > Al3+.
Ionisation energy rises across a period and falls down a group, with sharp jumps at core removals.
Electron affinity is most energy-releasing for the halogens; noble gases and group 2 resist electron gain.
Electronegativity peaks at fluorine and follows the same direction as ionisation energy.
Period 2 anomalies: nitrogen over oxygen, beryllium over boron, neon over fluorine.
Metallic character and electropositivity grow down a group and shrink across a period.
Diagonal relationships link Li–Mg, Be–Al and B–Si through similar charge-to-size ratios.
examFocus: Write a trend answer in three labelled parts: direction, reason in terms of shells against nuclear charge, one named example.
Quote the exception with its cause — half-filled sub-shell or electron-pair repulsion — rather than only stating it.
Successive ionisation energy data are read from the biggest jump, which tells you the group number directly.
For oxide character questions, give one basic, one amphoteric and one acidic oxide as evidence.

vocabulary.meaning: Regular recurrence of similar properties as atomic number increases.
Energy needed to remove one electron from one gaseous atom.
Energy released when one electron is added to one gaseous atom.
Ability of a bonded atom to attract the shared pair of electrons.
Species with the same number of electrons, such as O2− and F−.
Screening of outer electrons from the nucleus by inner-shell electrons.
Similarity shown by a period 2 element with the element below-right of it.
Element along the staircase with properties between metals and non-metals.
Combining capacity of an element, usually the number of unpaired valence electrons.
Apparent charge carried by an atom in a compound, based on electron assignment.

questions.prompt: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing:
questions.explanation: Moseley’s law sorts elements by atomic number, which increases regularly and never inverts as mass can.

questions.prompt: Which property increases steadily from sodium to chlorine across period 3?
questions.explanation: Nuclear charge rises with the same three shells, so removing an electron becomes progressively harder.

questions.prompt: Among N3−, O2−, F− and Na+, the species with the largest ionic radius is:
questions.explanation: All four are isoelectronic with 10 electrons, so the one with the fewest protons attracts them least and is largest.

questions.prompt: The first ionisation energy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen because:
options: Nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p sub-shell and oxygen loses a paired electron
Nitrogen has a higher mass number
questions.answer: Nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p sub-shell and oxygen loses a paired electron
questions.explanation: Three unpaired 2p electrons in a half-filled sub-shell resist removal, while oxygen’s fourth 2p electron is one of a repelling pair.

questions.prompt: The regular repetition of similar properties with increasing atomic number is called __________ .
questions.explanation: Periodicity arises because elements with the same valence-electron arrangement recur at fixed intervals.

questions.prompt: The energy released when one mole of gaseous atoms each gains one electron is called electron __________ .
questions.explanation: Electron affinity is measured for gaseous atoms and is most exothermic for the halogens.

questions.answer: The properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
questions.explanation: Atomic number fixes the electron arrangement, and the electron arrangement decides chemical behaviour.

questions.prompt: Explain why atomic radius decreases across a period although electrons are added.
questions.answer: Across a period every added electron enters the same outermost shell while protons are added to the nucleus. The shell count is unchanged, so the greater effective nuclear charge pulls the outer shell inward and the radius falls.
questions.explanation: Constant shielding with rising nuclear charge is the whole reason; the small increase in electron repulsion does not offset it.

questions.prompt: Define electronegativity and name the element that has the highest value.
questions.answer: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a bonded molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself; fluorine has the highest value, about 4.0 on the Pauling scale.
questions.explanation: It is a relative bonding property rather than an isolated-atom energy, which is why a scale rather than a joule figure is quoted.

questions.prompt: Describe how first ionisation energy varies across period 3 and account for the single reversal in the trend.
questions.answer: Ionisation energy generally rises from sodium to argon because the number of shells stays at three while nuclear charge increases, so the outer electrons are held more tightly. The rise is not smooth: aluminium has a slightly lower value than magnesium because its outer electron enters the higher-energy 3p sub-shell rather than the stable 3s^2 arrangement, and sulfur has a lower value than phosphorus because phosphorus has a half-filled 3p^3 sub-shell while sulfur’s fourth 3p electron is paired and repels its neighbour. Outside these two points the trend climbs steadily.
questions.explanation: The overall direction follows rising nuclear charge at constant shielding; each dip is explained by sub-shell energy or electron pairing.

questions.prompt: An element has the successive ionisation energies 590, 1150, 4940 and 6480 kJ mol^-1. Identify its group and predict the charge of its ion.
questions.answer: The first two removals cost similar amounts, both from valence electrons, while the third is more than four times the second, showing that the third electron comes from an inner shell. The element therefore has two valence electrons, belongs to group 2, and forms a 2+ ion. Magnesium fits these values.
questions.explanation: The group follows the count of electrons removed before the first large jump, which is the standard reading of ionisation data.

questions.prompt: Predict the formula and the acid-base character of the oxides of Na, Al and S, and justify each.
questions.answer: Sodium is strongly metallic, so Na2O is a basic oxide that dissolves to give sodium hydroxide. Aluminium sits on the staircase, so Al2O3 is amphoteric, reacting with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. Sulfur is a non-metal, so SO3 is acidic, dissolving in water to give sulphuric acid. Metallic character falls across the period, and oxide character follows it from basic through amphoteric to acidic.
questions.explanation: The oxide test is the practical expression of the metallic-character trend across a period.
